101.quote_or_event: “You bless me with everything, showering me with Mercy; And I am such an ungrateful wretch!”
101.explanation: Guru Arjan contrasts God's unearned, unceasing generosity with the human failure to acknowledge it; in Gurbani every blessing is grace, given before any merit of ours.
101.tie_back: Like the Kural's help given to one who had done nothing to deserve it, the Lord's gifts here are wholly unearned, and the only fitting response is a gratitude that can never repay them.
101.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 809, Raag Bilaaval, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
101._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on unearned benefaction and the debt of gratitude; the benefactor is God rather than a human helper, and the verse confesses ingratitude rather than stating the immeasurability of the gift.

102.quote_or_event: “Where there is no mother, father, children, friends or siblings - O my mind, there, only the Naam, the Name of the Lord, shall be with you as your help and support.”
102.explanation: In Sukhmani Sahib Guru Arjan praises the Naam as the help that arrives at the hour when every human support has fallen away.
102.tie_back: The Kural prizes help given at the moment of real need above the whole world; Gurbani likewise exalts the support that comes precisely when no one else can help.
102.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 264, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
102._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the stress on help at the critical moment, but the helper is the divine Name, not a human favour, and the verse does not speak of gratitude or of the help's small size.

103.quote_or_event: “One who performs selfless service, without thought of reward, shall attain his Lord and Master.”
103.explanation: Seva done nihkam, without desire for any return, is one of the central Sikh ideals; Sukhmani Sahib makes such service the path to God.
103.tie_back: The Kural's benefactor who helps without weighing the return is exactly the Sikh nihkam sevadar, though the Sikh verse praises the giver where the Kural asks the receiver to weigh the gift.
103.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 286, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
103._accuracy_note: Strong fit on help given without calculating reward; the Kural's point about the recipient's appraisal (greater than the ocean) has no counterpart in the verse.

104.quote_or_event: “Countless sins are erased, by even a tiny particle of the Lord's Name.”
104.explanation: Guru Amar Das uses a scale contrast: a mere particle of the Naam outweighs countless sins.
104.tie_back: The Kural's millet seed seen as a palm tree is a similar contrast of tiny and vast; Gurbani applies it to the immense worth of the smallest gift of grace.
104.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1283, Raag Malaar, Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
104._accuracy_note: Next-best: shares only the small-versus-immense image; the verse concerns the power of the Name, not the grateful person's magnifying of a small favour.

105.quote_or_event: Sikh tradition remembers that Amar Das, already an old man, became a disciple of Guru Angad and served him with extraordinary devotion for over a decade, fetching water before dawn and serving in the community kitchen; his humble service led Guru Angad to name him the third Guru in 1552.
105.explanation: The episode shows a disciple whose response to the grace he received was measured not by any calculation but by the depth of his own devotion.
105.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural's claim that the return for a benefit is bounded by the nobility of the one who received it rather than by the size of the benefit.
105.source: Wikipedia, 'Guru Amar Das' (paraphrase of traditional accounts)
105._accuracy_note: Next-best: a hagiographic tradition about devotion to the Guru rather than a teaching on gratitude's measure; Wikipedia used as last resort because the Britannica article checked does not narrate the service, and the details (years, water-fetching) are traditional.

106.quote_or_event: “They alone are my friends, who travel along with me; and in that place, where the accounts are called for, they appear standing with me.”
106.explanation: Guru Nanak defines the true friend as the one who stays beside you at the moment of reckoning, when everyone else falls away.
106.tie_back: The Kural's friend who was your strength in distress and must never be forsaken is the same kind of friend Guru Nanak names: one who stands by you when it counts.
106.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Raag Soohee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
106._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the friend proven in the hour of trial; Gurbani's 'friends' here are ultimately the virtues and the holy who accompany the soul, and the verse does not command remembering or not abandoning them.

107.quote_or_event: “A hundred times a day, I am a sacrifice to my Guru; He made angels out of men, without delay.”
107.explanation: Opening the Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak expresses unending gratitude to the Guru who transforms ordinary people; the disciple's thankfulness is renewed again and again.
107.tie_back: As the Kural's good remember through seven births the one who wiped away their sorrow, the Sikh offers ceaseless gratitude to the Guru who lifted him out of his lowly state.
107.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 462, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, Salok Mahala 1, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
107._accuracy_note: Reasonable-to-strong fit on lasting gratitude to a benefactor; the benefactor is the spiritual Guru, and the Sikh frame is not rebirth-based remembrance.

108.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
108.explanation: Bhagat Kabir places God's presence wherever there is forgiveness, khima, one of the virtues Gurbani asks of the Sikh.
108.tie_back: The Kural asks us to forget a wrong the same day it is done; Kabir's verse treats such forgiveness as the very place where God dwells.
108.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir 155 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
108._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: affirms forgiveness, but does not contain the Kural's asymmetry of remembering benefits while forgetting injuries.

109.quote_or_event: “He obtains ten things, and puts them behind him; for the sake of one thing withheld, he forfeits his faith. But what if that one thing were not given, and the ten were taken away? Then, what could the fool say or do?”
109.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the ungrateful person who forgets ten gifts because of one thing he did not receive.
109.tie_back: This is the Kural's moral calculus turned inside out: where the grateful let one remembered kindness erase a deadly injury, the ingrate lets one grievance erase ten kindnesses.
109.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 268, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
109._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit as a mirror image of the Kural; it criticises ingratitude toward God rather than counselling us to forgive a benefactor's later harm.

110.quote_or_event: “No one can save such an ungrateful person; he is thrown into the most horrible hell.”
110.explanation: Guru Arjan names the akirtghan, the one who forgets what has been done for him, as a person whom nothing can save.
110.tie_back: The Kural says any other sin may find expiation but not the killing of gratitude; Gurbani likewise singles out ingratitude as leaving one beyond rescue.
110.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1086, Raag Maaroo, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
110._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on ingratitude as beyond rescue; Gurbani elsewhere also says God cherishes and forgives even the ungrateful (e.g. Ang 47), so this is not the whole Sikh picture.
